1184.title: Where it's followed
1184.hook: Turkey, the Balkans, Central Asia, South Asia
1184.howItsDone: Hanafi Muslims across Turkey, the Balkans, Central Asia and South Asia follow the school's rulings on prayer, fasting and family law, and prayer timetables in mixed cities may list a separate Hanafi time for the afternoon prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Abu Yusuf and al-Shaybani, the two companions, and your line: students carry it.

On the wall of some mosques, and in some prayer apps, the afternoon prayer has two start times. Asr, standard. Asr, Hanafi. The Hanafi one comes later. Same sun, same city, same day. The difference is a shadow. In the Shafi'i, Maliki and Hanbali books, Asr begins when an object's shadow grows as long as the object. The Hanafi school, following Abu Hanifa's view, waits until it's twice as long. So a timetable for a city with both prints both lines, and each person knows which is theirs. That second line is a small map. It tells you the school traveled.
screen: `TWO TIMES FOR ONE PRAYER.` → `ONE SHADOW, OR TWO.` → `A TIMETABLE THAT IS A MAP.`

segments.voice: Back on day 110 you met the word madhhab: a way, a path someone takes. The Hanafi way left Kufa early. Abu Yusuf sat as a judge for the Abbasid caliphs in Baghdad, and judges trained in the school's books went out with the courts. Then empires carried it. The Ottomans made it the law of their courts, from Istanbul across Anatolia and the Balkans, so a Muslim in Sarajevo, Skopje or Istanbul is often praying the way the Hanafi books describe. In Central Asia, in cities like Bukhara and Samarkand, Hanafi scholars wrote major works of the school. In South Asia, the Mughal court commissioned a large collection of Hanafi rulings, the Fatawa 'Alamgiri, one reason the school is followed in Pakistan, India, Bangladesh and Afghanistan. Some writers call it the most followed school, pointing to the size of the regions it covers. There's no precise count, and some Muslims simply pray the way their parents and local mosque do, without naming a madhhab at all. And a map doesn't show this: in each of those places, Hanafis live beside Shafi'is, Malikis, Hanbalis and Ja'fari Shia, sometimes in the same mosque. Hence two lines for Asr on one wall. Each school is a way someone goes, and the ways cross.
screen: `MADHHAB: A WAY SOMEONE TAKES.` · `CARRIED BY COURTS AND EMPIRES.` · `ISTANBUL, BUKHARA, LAHORE, DHAKA.` · `THE WAYS CROSS IN ONE MOSQUE.`

segments.voice: Trace it on a map, real or in your mind: start in Kufa, go west to Istanbul and up to Sarajevo, east across the Caspian to Bukhara and Samarkand, then south through Afghanistan to Lahore, Delhi and Dhaka. In each city, picture one person standing for the afternoon prayer, a little later than their neighbor. If you pray, you can remember the Muslims of one of those cities by name.
Where it's followed. The Hanafi school runs through Turkey, the Balkans, Central Asia and South Asia, carried by its judges and by empires that made it the law of their courts. Today's word.
Your line: the most followed school. From Kufa to Dhaka, carried by courts and judges. Until tomorrow.

1185.title: He refused a judgeship
1185.hook: reports say Abu Hanifa refused to be a judge for the caliph and was imprisoned
1185.howItsDone: Muslim biographers tell of Abu Hanifa refusing the judgeship under pressure, and of other scholars who avoided the post out of fear of judging wrongly, while honoring those who took it and judged justly.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Hanafi map, from Istanbul to Dhaka, and your line: the most followed school.

The offer comes with power: a judgeship, with the caliph's backing, over property, marriages and punishments. The man being offered it is a cloth merchant and a teacher with students of his own in Kufa. He says no. He's asked again, and he says no again. The reports differ on the details, but they agree on the shape: the pressure grew, and so did the price of refusing. His school would go on to fill courts. The founder himself would not sit in the judge's seat.
screen: `A POST WITH POWER.` → `HE SAYS NO, AND NO AGAIN.` → `THE PRICE OF REFUSING.`

segments.voice: His biographers tell of a governor of Iraq who wanted him as a judge and had him beaten when he refused, and of the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur pressing him again and having him imprisoned. Some reports say he died in that prison. The accounts don't all agree, and historians weigh them differently, so it's fair to say: this is what the reports say. Then a story people tell. Abu Hanifa told the caliph he wasn't fit for the post. You're lying, said the caliph. Then you've just ruled that I'm unfit, he answered, because a liar can't be a judge. Whether or not it happened in those words, it shows how he's remembered: quick, calm, impossible to corner. Why refuse at all? A hadith in Sunan Abi Dawud says whoever is made a judge among people has been slaughtered without a knife. Scholars read it as a warning that judging endangers the soul: a wrong ruling could take someone's home or someone's life. Some pious scholars ran from the post for that reason. Others, like Abu Yusuf, accepted it and tried to judge justly, and the tradition honors them too. Readers see one more reason: a judge appointed by a ruler can be pushed by that ruler. Refusing kept Abu Hanifa's judgment his own, while the school he built went on to staff courts across empires.
screen: `WHAT THE REPORTS SAY.` · `YOU'VE JUST RULED THAT I'M UNFIT.` · `SLAUGHTERED WITHOUT A KNIFE.` · `KEEPING HIS JUDGMENT HIS OWN.`

segments.voice: Think of a role someone wants you to take that doesn't fit: covering for a friend, taking sides in a family fight, a yes that would cost something you won't trade. Find the sentence you'd use to say no, short and kind, and say it once in your head, noticing your shoulders as you do; if the role turns out to be right after all, notice that too. If you pray, you can ask for steadiness.

1186.title: Malik ibn Anas
1186.hook: the imam of Medina, who would not ride in the Prophet's city out of respect (reported)
1186.howItsDone: Maliki Muslims remember Imam Malik as the scholar of Medina who taught hadith with great reverence and was willing to say 'I don't know'; his school is followed in North and West Africa.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Abu Hanifa and the judge's seat he would not take. Your line: he refused the post.

Fine horses stand tied outside a scholar's door in Medina. Gifts, he explains to a visiting student. The student asks the natural question: then why not ride one? The answer, as his biographers tell it: he would be ashamed before Allah to tread with a hoof on ground where the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ lies buried. So in the Prophet's city, he walked. The student is said to be a young al-Shafi'i, whom you'll meet properly soon. The man on foot founded the next school on this path. Today: Malik ibn Anas.
screen: `HORSES AT THE DOOR.` → `WHY NOT RIDE ONE?` → `IN THE PROPHET'S CITY, HE WALKED.`

segments.voice: Abu Hanifa was a man of Kufa, a busy city of merchants and debates. Malik was a man of Medina, where the Prophet lived, prayed, taught and was buried. He was born there, taught there and, the reports say, rarely left except for pilgrimage. Hence the imam of Medina. His biographers say that before teaching hadith he would wash, put on good clothes and perfume, and sit with dignity, because the words were the Prophet's. A story people tell has a scorpion stinging him again and again during a lesson, and Malik not stopping until the hadith was finished. Whether every detail is exact, the picture holds: he treated the Prophet's words like a guest of honor. Then his honesty. A traveler is said to have come a long way with a list of questions, and Malik answered question after question with two words: la adri, I don't know. The man protested that he'd come so far. Malik's reply, in the report: tell people that Malik doesn't know. For a jurist, I don't know was a form of respect too. Last, a line attributed to him, pointing at the Prophet's grave: everyone's word can be taken or left, except the one in this grave. Some reports give versions of it to others. Either way, it fits the man: careful with the Prophet's city, careful with his words, and careful with his own.
screen: `THE IMAM OF MEDINA.` · `WASHED AND PERFUMED TO TEACH HADITH.` · `LA ADRI: I DON'T KNOW.` · `EVERYONE'S WORD, EXCEPT ONE.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand and walk a few slow steps around your room; if not, walk in your mind into a place that deserves care, a grave you've visited, a house of worship, your grandmother's kitchen. Notice your feet, your pace, your voice getting lower, what you'd touch and what you wouldn't, then stand still for a moment. If you pray, you can greet that place with a greeting your tradition uses.

1187.title: The Muwatta
1187.hook: the trodden path, one of the earliest books of law and hadith
1187.howItsDone: Muslims study the Muwatta of Imam Malik as a book of hadith and law, and in Maliki lands it has long been taught in mosques and schools, usually in the transmission of Yahya ibn Yahya al-Laythi.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Malik ibn Anas, on foot in the Prophet's city, saying I don't know. Your line: the imam of medina.

A path across open ground, pressed flat by feet until the walking is easy. Nobody laid it out with a ruler; people walking it made it. Malik ibn Anas gave his book a name with that picture in it: al-Muwatta, usually translated the well-trodden path, or the path made smooth. Not a new road cut by one man, but a road already walked: by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, by his companions, by the people of Medina after them. Page by page, the book reads like a record of where those feet went.
screen: `A PATH PRESSED FLAT BY FEET.` → `A NAME WITH THAT PICTURE IN IT.` → `A ROAD ALREADY WALKED.`

segments.voice: Tradition counts it among the earliest written books of Islamic law and hadith still in our hands. And it isn't only a list of hadith. Malik arranges it by topic, the way a law book is: purity, prayer, fasting, pilgrimage, trade, marriage, and on through daily life. Under each topic come sayings of the Prophet, then rulings of his companions, then what the people after them did, and often Malik's own comment: this is the practice among us here in Medina. That phrase is tomorrow's whole lesson. How did it reach us? Malik taught the book for years, and different students wrote down what they heard, so the Muwatta comes in more than one transmission. The version of Yahya ibn Yahya al-Laythi, who carried it to Spain, is widely read today. Another comes through al-Shaybani, the Hanafi student from last week, who also studied with Malik. Near the end, in the book on good character, Malik records that the Prophet said he was sent to perfect good character. A book of law, purity and trade, and close to its end, a line about who you are with people. It's a fair summary of the path: the rules are walked so the person comes out better.
screen: `AL-MUWATTA: THE WELL-TRODDEN PATH.` · `ARRANGED BY TOPIC, LIKE A LAW BOOK.` · `MORE THAN ONE TRANSMISSION.` · `SENT TO PERFECT GOOD CHARACTER.`

segments.voice: Say the line from the book on good character slowly, once: the Prophet said that he was sent to perfect good character. Then picture a path your feet know, from your front door to somewhere you go every day, and ask what one small piece of good character would look like, walked that often: a greeting at the same door, a thank-you to the same driver. If you pray, you can carry the line into your prayer.
The Muwatta. Malik's book of law and hadith, arranged by topic; its name is usually translated the well-trodden path. Today's word.

1188.title: The practice of Medina
1188.hook: Malik gave weight to the living practice of Medina's people
1188.howItsDone: Maliki jurists treat the settled practice of the people of Medina as strong evidence of the Prophet's sunnah, at times preferring it over a report carried by a single narrator.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Muwatta, Malik's book arranged by topic. Your line: the well-trodden path.

In the Muwatta's chapter on trade, Malik records a saying of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: a buyer and a seller each keep the right to call off the deal as long as they haven't parted. Right under it, Malik adds a note. Among us, he says, there's no fixed limit for this, and no practice of acting on it. He has just written the hadith down himself, carefully, with its chain. And in the same breath he says Medina doesn't do it that way. That isn't carelessness. It's a method, and it's the heart of his school.
screen: `A HADITH ON CALLING OFF A SALE.` → `MALIK'S NOTE: NOT DONE HERE.` → `NOT CARELESS: A METHOD.`

segments.voice: The phrase is 'amal ahl al-Madinah, the practice of the people of Medina. Medina was where the Prophet lived his last years, where the companions prayed behind him and traded in his market. Their children watched them, and their grandchildren watched their children. So what Medina did, day after day, was itself a kind of report: not one person remembering one sentence, but a whole city carrying a way of life from parent to child. For Malik, where the settled practice of Medina went one way and a single narrator's report went another, the practice could carry more weight. The report might be true but limited, or later set aside, and the city's daily life would know. That's what the note under the trade hadith is doing. Then a friendly argument. Al-Layth ibn Sa'd, a great scholar of Egypt, wrote Malik a letter of real respect and real disagreement. The companions, he said, didn't all stay in Medina. They went to Egypt, Syria and Iraq, and taught there too. Medina's practice is precious, but it isn't the only living practice. Malik's school kept its method; the letter was preserved, and readers still point to it as scholars disagreeing well. Some knowledge lives on paper. Some lives in how people stand, greet, trade and pray. Malik took the second kind seriously enough to build a school on it.
screen: `'AMAL AHL AL-MADINAH.` · `A WHOLE CITY AS A REPORT.` · `AL-LAYTH: THE COMPANIONS WENT ELSEWHERE TOO.` · `KNOWLEDGE THAT LIVES IN PRACTICE.`

If you pray, you can remember the people who taught you without meaning to.

1189.title: North and West Africa
1189.hook: the Maliki school is followed from Morocco to Nigeria, often praying with hands at the sides
1189.howItsDone: Across North and West Africa, Maliki Muslims often pray with their arms at their sides (sadl), while some fold their hands; both are found in Maliki mosques.

segments.voice: Yesterday: 'amal ahl al-Madinah, Medina's settled way of life. Your line: the living practice.

A row of worshipers stands shoulder to shoulder in a mosque in Fez, or Dakar, or Kano. The imam says Allahu akbar and the prayer begins. Look along the row at their hands. Some are folded over the chest or the stomach. Others hang straight down, loose at the sides, the whole way through the standing. A visitor from Istanbul or Lahore might wonder if something was forgotten. Nothing was. Those loose hands are a quiet signature of Malik's school, carried a long way from Medina.
screen: `A ROW OF WORSHIPERS IN FEZ.` → `SOME HANDS FOLDED, SOME AT THE SIDES.` → `NOTHING WAS FORGOTTEN.`

segments.voice: The Maliki school traveled west from Medina, along the North African coast and across the Sahara. Today it's followed in Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia and Libya, in Mauritania, and through West Africa, in Senegal, Mali and northern Nigeria, among other places. Scholars carried it: teachers in Kairouan in Tunisia, students in Spain, and later the scholars of Timbuktu, with their manuscript libraries. Back on day 110 you met different hands in one prayer. Here's the Maliki side. The posture is called sadl, letting the arms hang. In the Mudawwana, an early Maliki book recording Malik's answers, he's reported to have disliked folding the hands in the obligatory prayer. Maliki scholars give reasons: it was the practice they received in Medina, and it guards against leaning or showing off. Then the honest complication. Malik's own Muwatta records a report that people were told to place the right hand over the left in prayer. So some Malikis fold their hands, and they too point to Malik. Both postures are found in Maliki mosques, sometimes in the same row. The other Sunni schools fold their hands, in slightly different places, and Shia Muslims pray with their arms at their sides too. Each can tell you why. And the prayer behind the imam is one prayer, whatever the hands are doing.

1190.title: Imam al-Shafi'i
1190.hook: a descendant of the Prophet's clan, who studied with Malik and the Hanafis
1190.howItsDone: Shafi'i Muslims, across places such as Egypt, East Africa, Yemen and Southeast Asia, follow the school of Imam al-Shafi'i, who studied with Malik in Medina and with Hanafi scholars in Iraq.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Maliki lands of North and West Africa, and sadl. Your line: hands at the sides.

A young man arrives in Medina already knowing a book by heart. It's Malik's Muwatta, and the story goes that he memorized it before he ever met its author. He sits in Malik's circle and reads it back to him. Years later he's in Iraq, reading the books of al-Shaybani, Abu Hanifa's student, and arguing with the Hanafis face to face. Medina's way and Kufa's way both pass through one mind. What comes out is a third school, and a new way of asking how law should be found at all.
screen: `THE MUWATTA, BY HEART.` → `MALIK'S CIRCLE, THEN IRAQ.` → `BOTH WAYS THROUGH ONE MIND.`

segments.voice: His name is Muhammad ibn Idris, called al-Shafi'i after an ancestor named Shafi'. He was of Quraysh, the Prophet's tribe, from the line of al-Muttalib, a brother of Hashim, who was great-grandfather to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. So the two family trees meet a few generations back. Yet his biographers say he grew up an orphan, poor, in Mecca, with a mother who couldn't afford paper. He learned the Qur'an and Arabic in Mecca, then studied with Malik in Medina. Later, in Iraq, he studied the Hanafi books, and tradition says he learned from al-Shaybani in person. He had sat with the imam of Medina and read the people of reasoned judgment closely: learned from both. He didn't simply blend them. He asked what each was doing and why, and wrote it down as a method. From Malik he kept the hadith at the center; from the Hanafis, careful reasoning. He argued with both, and ended his days in Egypt, where his tomb stands in Cairo. Look back over these days: two times for Asr, a judge's seat refused, I don't know in Medina, the well-trodden path, the living practice, hands at the sides. Now a student who carried Kufa and Medina, and asked how they fit. The Qur'an gives a short line for students like him: my Lord, increase me in knowledge.
screen: `OF QURAYSH, AN ORPHAN IN MECCA.` · `MALIK IN MEDINA, THE HANAFIS IN IRAQ.` · `NOT A BLEND: A METHOD.` · `A WEEK OF TWO SCHOOLS, AND A THIRD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind two people who taught you the same thing in different ways: two grandparents cooking the same dish, two coaches, a parent who explained and a parent who showed. Notice what each got right, where they disagreed, and how much of each is in what you do today. If you pray, you can say the line from Surah Ta Ha, My Lord! Increase me in knowledge; if not, simply rest with both faces in mind.
